د عضوي مرکباتو د شمېر له زیاتېدو سره دومره ډېرو عضوي مرکباتو ته نومونه ورکول ناممکن شول. سربېره پر دې، دودیز نومونه د مرکباتو د جوړښت په اړه هېڅ معلومات نه ورکوي. له همدې امله په منظم ډول د عضوي مرکباتو د نومولو اړتیا احساس شوه. نو “د خالصې او تطبیقي کیمیا نړیوالې اتحادیې” (IUPAC) په 1957 کې د جوړښت پر بنسټ عضوي مرکباتو ته د منظمو نومونو ورکولو اصول وټاکل. دا د نومولو IUPAC سیستم بلل کېږي.

16.2.1.1 د الکانونو نومول

الکانونه د عام او IUPAC دواړو سیستمونو له مخې نومول کېږي.

(a) عام سیستم

د لړۍ لومړي څلور غړي میتان (CH₄)، ایتان (C₂H₆)، پروپان (C₃H₈) او بیوټان (C₄H₁₀) نومېږي، خو پاتې غړي په یوناني مختاړو نومول کېږي چې په مالیکول کې د کاربني اټومونو شمېر ښيي. نو د پنځو کاربني اټومونو لرونکي مرکب لپاره پینټ (5)، د شپږو لپاره هېکس (6)، د اوو لپاره هېپټ (7)، د اتو لپاره اوکټ (8)، د نهو لپاره نون (9) او د لسو کاربني اټومونو لپاره ډېک (10) مختاړی کارېږي. Alkynes and Cycloalkynes

2. Aromatic Hydrocarbons

The term aromatic was derived from the Greek word aroma (fragrant), because of their pleasant smell. Aromatic hydrocarbons, were typically obtained by treatment of pleasant-smelling plant extracts. Another name for aromatic hydrocarbons is arenes. Benzene (C₆H₆) is the parent member of this class and hence aromatic is the term used for benzene and all those compounds that resemble benzene in their chemical properties. Over time, chemists discovered that many derivatives of benzene are, in fact, odorless. Nevertheless, the term aromatic is still used to describe all derivatives of benzene, regardless of whether they are fragrant or odourless. Examples of some aromatic hydrocarbons are given below.

16.2 Alkanes and Cycloalkanes

Alkanes are open chain saturated hydrocarbons, which can be represented by the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (where “n” is the number of carbon atoms), while cycloalkanes are cyclic saturated hydrocarbons represented by the general formula CₙH₂ₙ (n > 2). It is to be noted from the general formula of cycloalkanes, that there are two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes. In cycloalkanes, two carbon atoms of the molecule utilize one of their valency in forming bonds with other carbon atoms for formation of cyclic ring.

Tidbit

An aromatic organic compound is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated compound containing (4n+2) pi electrons; where n should be 0, 1, 2, 3 …

16.2.1 Nomenclature

The naming of organic compounds is called Organic Nomenclature. Nomenclature in organic chemistry is of two types: common (or trivial) and systematic (or IUPAC system). At the beginning of organic chemistry, each new compound was given an individual name, which was based on its source, some property or other trivial reason. For example, the compound HCOOH was given the name formic acid. The name formic acid was derived from Latin word formica meaning ant, because it was obtained from red ants. Such names, which are based on the source of the compounds are called common names or trivial names.

With the increase in the number of organic compounds it became impossible to give names to such a large number of organic compounds. Moreover, trivial names do not give any information about the structure of the compounds. Need was, therefore, felt to name organic compounds in a systematic way. Thus, the “International Union of pure and Applied chemistry” (IUPAC) in 1957, set rules for giving systematic names to organic compounds on the basis of structure. This is known as the IUPAC system of nomenclature.

16.2.1.1 Nomenclature of Alkanes

Alkanes are named by both common and IUPAC systems.

(a) Common System

The first four members of the series are named as methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀) while the rest are named by using the Greek prefixes that indicate number of carbon atoms in the molecule. Thus the prefix pent (5) is used for the compound having five carbon atoms, hex (6) for six, hept (7) for seven, oct (8) for eight, non (9) for nine and dec (10) for ten carbon atoms. (see table 16.1). The suffix “–ane” should be added with above prefixes for complete name.
